messages.subject: .First.lib problem
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am having the following problem and asking for help. This is S-plus
6.1 on Windows. This is about a library section called GWS with
.First.lib:

.First.lib <- function(library,section){
create.menu.gws()     
dyn.open("C:\\PROGRA~1\\INSIGH~1\\splus61\\library\\GWS\\S.dll")
library(MASS)
}

where "create.menu.gws()" is to create GUI menus and the second line
loads a dll compiled from some Fortran code. The reason to have
"library(MASS)" is that library GWS uses a function in MASS. However it
seems that "library(MASS)" does not work, so I have to manually load it.
But I thought this is one way to load MASS when library GWS is loaded.
In addition, if I issued

>.First.lib()

then I got the error:

Problem in .First.lib(): Argument "" is missing, with no default. 

If I commented out "library(MASS)", then there was no such error.

Maybe this is totally wrong, but what is a right way to load MASS
automatically?

Thanks,
 
--

I am trying to do multiple comparisons for the means at different conditions

 

I started the analysis with SAS using proc mixed which require me to model
lung function. The SAS code is attached below:

 

PROC MIXED DATA=lung;

  CLASS Subject condtion ;

  MODEL lung function = condtion;

  REPEATED  condtion /TYPE=CS SUBJECT=SUB ;

  lsmeans   condtion /pdiff ADJUST=bon;

run;

 

I noticed that the estimated means from the analysis @ any condition are
different from mean which I get by averaging the lung function value @ the same
condition. Thus this analysis is different from multiple paired t-test which I am
trying to do. 

 

My questions are

works if you give it arguments -- that you do not get an error message 
with library(MASS) commented out does not mean it `there is no such

its .First.lib will abort the process before the last line.  And it does 
not need that dyn.open line as S.dll is automatically loaded.

messages.subject: Re: .First.lib problem
messages.body_plain:
For your information, S-PLUS can distinguish between a character vector
and a function.  So as I stated, if this .First.lib function is called as
documented it will work since it knows to look for a function and not a
character vector.  That it cannot distinguish between a missing argument
and a function should be regarded as a bug, especially as I am pretty sure
earlier versions used to be able to.  Nevertheless, the error is the 
user's in not calling the function as documented and not in the argument 
naming.

.First.lib *is* documented to have arguments `library' and `section', so
it is dangerous to suggest that they should be renamed.  One day a careful
programmer may call it as .First.lib(library="foo", section="GWS"), which
is documented to work.

BTW, it is regarded as courteous to copy to people your reply to their 
posting, as I am doing.

messages.subject: Re: NLM question
messages.body_plain:
I don't know "NLM", but if I were my problem, I'd first select a 
set of values for k > max(x), then run lm(ln(k-x)~y) for each one, store 
the residual standard deviations s.e(k) and plot them vs. k.  From this, 
you can get a 95% confidence interval on k as follows:  Suppose you have 
N observations.  This procedure in effect estimates 3 parameters, the 
intercept and slope of the regression on y plus k.  A 95% confidence 
region on k will be given by s.e(k)^2 > min(s.e(k)^2)*(1+pf(0.95, 1, 
N-3)). 

     If I had a hundred of these to do, I might investigate nls (and 
after I mastered that, nlme), parameterizing the problem as 
log(exp(ln.kx)+max(x)-x)~y, and estimate ln.kx.  See, e.g., the 
documentation for nls plus the following: 

     Bates and Watts (1988) Nonlinear Regression Analysis and Its 
Applications (Wiley)

     Chambers and Hastie (1992) Statistical Models in S (Wadsworth)

     I'd work the examples in the "nls" documentation very carefully 
and make sure I understood them.  Then I'd check www.r-project.org -> 
Search -> R site search -> profile.nls, use that search to find 
documentation for "profile", then "profile.nls" then "nls", work all the 
examples I found in that documentation, etc. 

     After that, I'd investigate Pinheiro and Bates (2000) 
Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-Plus for the nlme function, etc. 

     hope this helps.  spencer graves

messages.body_plain:
Helen,

I am using Splus 6.0. The "det" functions looks like this:
--------------------------------------------------------
det
function(x)
{
     z <- determinant(x, logarithm = T)
     z$sign * exp(z$modulus@.Data)
}

So it does not have an argument called "log". That's why Splus complains
that: "argument log=not matched:" for your code  It is the function
"determinant" that has an argument for logarithm.

By the way, do you understand what your code
"d<-det(as.Matrix(somme),log=F)" wants to do?  If you just want to get the
determinant,  simply uses  "d<-det(as.Matrix(somme))" will give you the
right result. You can do some testing yourself to convince yourself.

Good luck.

Max Zhao

Thanks to Sean 
Keenan, Tim Hesterberg, Tom Jagger, Julia Reid, Manoel Pacheco, Jean Adams,

df4 <-

for some reason I

good <- 
is.element(...)

df4 <- 
df2[!good,]

hitting a wrong key when I tried !is.element.....

messages.body_plain:
I ranked a list of chemicals by two distinct variables (one is a "Standard"
and the other a surrogate), and made an initial attempt to compare the two
sets of ranks by computing the sum of absolute differences between them.
Next, I generated random permutations of the "standard" ranks and computed
the sum of absolute differences between them. The random permutation of
ranks was performed with the code below:

        dif <- vector("numeric",10000)
        rstand <- rank(Standard)
        for (i in 1:10000) {
            smp <- sample(rstand, replace=FALSE)
            dif[i] <- sum(abs(smp-rstand)
            }

       randif <- sort(dif)

The observed difference between ranks based on the standard and the
surrogate variable was less than the lowest value computed from the random
permutation of ranks, suggesting that the surrogate variable is adequate. Is
there a more elegant way to compare the two sets of ranks?

        Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
>I ranked a list of chemicals by two distinct variables (one is a "Standard"
>and the other a surrogate), and made an initial attempt to compare the two
>sets of ranks by computing the sum of absolute differences between them.
>Next, I generated random permutations of the "standard" ranks and computed
>the sum of absolute differences between them. The random permutation of
>ranks was performed with the code below:
>
>        dif <- vector("numeric",10000)
>        rstand <- rank(Standard)
>        for (i in 1:10000) {
>            smp <- sample(rstand, replace=FALSE)
>            dif[i] <- sum(abs(smp-rstand)
>            }
>
>       randif <- sort(dif)
>
>The observed difference between ranks based on the standard and the
>surrogate variable was less than the lowest value computed from the random
>permutation of ranks, suggesting that the surrogate variable is adequate. Is
>there a more elegant way to compare the two sets of ranks?

I think you have a subtle error there; you should generate
random permutations of the Surrogate ranks, for comparing to the
standard ranks.  E.g.
  dif <- vector("numeric",10000)
  rstand <- rank(Standard)
  rSurrogate <- rank(Surrogate)
  for (i in 1:10000) {
      smp <- sample(rSurrogate, replace=FALSE)
      dif[i] <- sum(abs(smp-rstand)
      }

This matters if there are ties.

It is also conceptually cleaner -- you want to compare the
value of an observed statistic with the same statistic computed
under permutations.  Your observed statistic is
        sum(abs(rank(Standard) - rank(Surrogate)))
so your comparison should be:
        sum(abs(rank(Standard) - rank(permuted version of Surrogate)))
not
        sum(abs(rank(Standard) - rank(permuted version of Standard)))

--------------------------------------------------
Back to your original question,
you could use the inner product of the two sets of ranks
(this is equivalent in a permutation test to the correlation
between ranks),
or inner product between normal scores computed from each rank,
e.g. qnorm(rstand/(length(rstand)+1))

--------------------------------------------------
Finally,
Whatever statistic you choose, you may use permutationTest
to do the calculations, e.g.

permResults <- permutationTest( rSurrogate, sum(abs(rSurrogate - rstand)))
permResults
plot(permResults)

permutationTest() is part of the resample library, see below.

messages.subject: Re: generating function arguments as string
messages.body_plain:
A simple way to do what you ask is found in almost all the modeling
functions (lm, coxph, etc).

  At the top of the function, before manipulating any arguments, you
will find the line

        call <- match.call()
        
Then the "call" component is added to the output.  It contains a copy of the
what you typed to invoke the function.  So

        fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + height, data=mydata, x=T)
        
The phrase
        refit <- eval(fit$call)
will re-fit the model as originally specified.
        fit$call
will print the original call on the screen.

        Terry Therneau

Can anybody suggest a simple way of doing this?

Thanks

Carlos Alzola

This is how I would do it. First, spin out your data so that there is 
one row for each patient. The first column is the original score, the 
second column is after the intervention. (I am using x for your original

matrix shft.a.i.)

x<-shft.a.i
xlong<-data.frame(cbind(rep(as.numeric(dimnames(x)[[1]]),rowSums(x)),rep
(rep(as.numeric(dimnames(x)[[2]]),rep(nrow(x),ncol(x))),as.vector(x))))
dimnames(xlong)[[2]]<-c("score1","score2")

plot(xlong$score1, xlong$score2, xlab="Initial score", ylab="Score after

intervention", xlim=c(0,12), ylim=c(0,12), type="n") text(xlong$score1,
xlong$score2, pch="*", labels=as.vector(x[x!=0]))

Hope this helps.
Julia

messages.subject: Re: tree function in R language
messages.body_plain:
Have you read the (latest edition of the) book for which the package you are
using supports?  There are differences in S-PLUS and R (and the 4th edition
of MASS supports both, thus ought to tell you this particular difference
between the two).  tree() in S-PLUS is written originally by Clark and
Pregibon.  If you want that functionality in R, you need to load the `tree'
package (available on CRAN), which is an independent implementation by one
of the co-authors of MASS.

Another hint: Look in the `scripts' subdirectory of where the `MASS' package
is installed.

Andy

`if' is not a vectorised function yet you supplied a vector to it. The 
warning implies `smax < s' is a vector of length 2. Perhaps you want 
something like

if(all(smax < s))

or

if(any(smax < s))

However if you are not expecting smax and/or s to have length greater 
than one, then you need to investigate how these objects are created.

--sundar

messages.subject: analysis of covariance question
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I have an S-Plus ANCOVA model where one variable is both included as a factor
and as a linear covariate within the same model, such that, e.g.:

model <- response ~ Xlinear + Xfactor

the underlying dataframe would,e.g., look like:

response Xlinear Xfactor
1.5         1      "one"
1.8         2      "two"
1.3         3      "three"

and so on. The reason why I´m doing this is because I want to test for linear
trends and for principal differences between the factor levels for the variable
of interest within one and the same model. Model simplification (using
"update") would then lead to the most parsimonous model.

My question now is: Is a procedure like this "allowed" or do I violate any basic
ANCOVA assumptions in fitting the model as described above?

Thanks for your help!
Best regards
Christoph.

I happened to have the same problem as yours some time ago.  Here is what I do:

Step 0.  Close your Splus session.

Step 1.  Use Window Explorer to go to your default working directory (the directory when you start up your Splus).
